summary: Describes LSP stitching in GMPLS TE, combining several label switched paths into a single end-to-end path, where each piece belongs to only one end-to-end path. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Short roads are linked end to end to form one long road, with each short road used for only one long journey.

questions: how to join label switched paths
what is an s-lsp in gmpls
how does gmpls lsp stitching signaling work
subtitle: How to join several GMPLS label switched paths into one end-to-end path, with each piece dedicated to a single end-to-end path.

tldr.problem: Operators sometimes need to combine several GMPLS label switched paths into one end-to-end path, but the existing hierarchy mechanism lets many paths share one carrier path and does not fit same-layer joining.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines LSP stitching: a head end signals 'LSP stitching desired' on a segment (S-LSP) using a new LSP_ATTRIBUTES flag, the egress answers 'LSP segment stitching ready', and an end-to-end LSP is then signaled across the segment, which is dedicated to that one LSP.
tldr.outcome: It gives GMPLS TE a standards-track way to stitch an end-to-end LSP across segments, useful for inter-domain signaling and for bypassing legacy nodes. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 5150 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What LSP Stitching Is
sections.content:
A stitched GMPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) Label Switched Path (LSP) is built from several LSP segments (S-LSPs) that are connected in the data plane, so that one end-to-end (e2e) LSP results. The key requirement is that a constituent LSP is not allocated to more than one e2e LSP.

The RFC defines the concept and the control plane mechanisms, both routing and signaling, to achieve it. It also points out where stitching is similar to or different from LSP hierarchy (RFC 4206).

A node could also be configured by management intervention to switch traffic from an LSP it ends onto another LSP it starts, with no protocol extensions. This RFC does not cover that case. With the mechanism defined here, the stitching node does not need the pair of S-LSPs configured in advance, and the result is an e2e LSP in both the control and data planes.
sections.eli5: Stitching means sticking several short paths together so they act like one long path. Each short path is used for only one long path.

sections.title: Stitching Versus LSP Hierarchy
sections.content:
LSP hierarchy lets a Hierarchical LSP (H-LSP) appear as a data link to LSPs in a higher layer, and many LSPs can be nested into one H-LSP. Each nested LSP exchanges a unique label over the H-LSP hop and may reserve some of its bandwidth.

An S-LSP is the 'moral equivalent' of an H-LSP, but it provides a data link to other LSPs in the same layer. At most one LSP may be stitched to an S-LSP. The whole S-LSP bandwidth is allocated to that LSP. Like an H-LSP, an S-LSP may be advertised as a TE link, and several S-LSPs may be bundled into one TE link (RFC 4201).

Unlike an H-LSP, there is no forwarding adjacency between the end points of an S-LSP TE link. In the control plane there is one RSVP session for the e2e LSP and one for each S-LSP, and targeted (non-adjacent) RSVP signaling from RFC 4206 is required.
sections.eli5: A nesting path is like a big truck that carries many small cars at once. A stitched segment is like a private lane given to just one car.

sections.title: Triggers and Uses
sections.content:
An S-LSP can be created by administrative control (configuration) or dynamically because of an incoming LSP request. The region-boundary trigger that RFC 4206 uses for forwarding adjacency LSPs MUST NOT be used for S-LSPs, because for stitching the switching capabilities of the previous hop and next hop TE links MUST be the same. Local policies SHOULD be used for dynamic creation instead.

Stitching applies when an e2e LSP must be tied to an S-LSP of the same switching type, so hierarchy does not apply. For example, an e2e lambda LSP over a lambda-switch capable segment cannot use hierarchy. The RFC names other uses: stitching an inter-domain e2e LSP to an intra-domain S-LSP, and bypassing legacy nodes, for instance stitching a point-to-multipoint RSVP LSP to a segment between P2MP-capable routers. It warns that the latter may limit the attractiveness of RSVP P2MP and should be examined before deployment.
sections.eli5: You use stitching when the pieces are the same kind of road, so you cannot stack one inside another. It also lets you skip over old equipment that cannot do new tricks.

sections.title: Routing Aspects
sections.content:
An S-LSP is created between two GMPLS nodes and may cross zero or more intermediate nodes. The end points look adjacent in the TE topology, but have no adjacency in the data plane. Traffic reaching the head end is switched into the S-LSP with a label swap.

An S-LSP MAY be treated as a TE link, numbered or unnumbered, and its TE information MAY be flooded by IS-IS TE or OSPF-TE. Advertising it is not required, and doing so adds to the size and complexity of the link-state database. The switching capability of the TE link MUST equal the switching type of the S-LSP.

An S-LSP MUST NOT admit more than one e2e LSP. Once it is allocated, its unreserved bandwidth SHOULD be set to zero so that path computation does not pick it again. For bundled S-LSPs, the component's unreserved bandwidth is zeroed and the Minimum and Maximum LSP bandwidth of the TE link SHOULD be recalculated.
sections.eli5: Once a private lane is given to a car, the map marks it as full so no other car is sent there.

sections.title: Signaling Procedures
sections.content:
The end nodes of an S-LSP SHOULD have a signaling adjacency (an RSVP neighbor relationship), even if they have no routing adjacency. Stitching is a two-step process: prepare the S-LSP, then stitch the e2e LSP to it.

Preparing the segment. The head end sets a new LSP stitching desired bit in the Attributes Flags TLV of the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object in the Path message. Other nodes MUST NOT modify it and nodes other than the egress SHOULD ignore it. An egress that is ready allocates a non-NULL label and sets a new LSP segment stitching ready bit in the RRO Attributes subobject. An egress that recognizes the request but cannot support it MUST send a PathErr with code Routing Problem and value Stitching unsupported. The ingress MUST NOT use the S-LSP for stitching if the ready bit is cleared.

Stitching the e2e LSP. The e2e switching type MUST equal the S-LSP switching type. The node uses the RFC 4206 procedures to send the e2e Path message to the segment end point, identifying the S-LSP in the RSVP_HOP. Because there is no forwarding adjacency, labels exchanged across the S-LSP hop have no significance: the egress MUST ignore an Upstream Label, and the ingress MUST ignore the Label in the Resv. If the S-LSP bandwidth is already taken, normal RSVP-TE pre-emption rules apply.

For packet LSPs using Penultimate Hop Popping, if the S-LSP egress is also the e2e egress, it sends a Resv trigger for the S-LSP with an Implicit or Explicit NULL label. For the route record, the e2e LSP SHOULD record an identifier of the S-LSP TE link, and SHOULD NOT record the intermediate hops of the segment.

Teardown. S-LSP teardown SHOULD be treated as a failure of the associated e2e LSP. Teardown of the two kinds of LSP is independent. When an e2e PathTear arrives at the stitching node it MUST be IP routed to the segment egress, with Router Alert off and the RSVP TTL check disabled. If an S-LSP was set up dynamically it MAY be torn down when unused, and a delay is RECOMMENDED, with 30 seconds as the RECOMMENDED interval.
sections.eli5: First the two ends of the short road ask each other, 'Are you ready to be joined?' When both say yes, the long journey is sent through. The labels inside the short road do not matter, so both ends just ignore them.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example has an e2e LSP, LSP1-2, from node R1 to node R2, and an S-LSP, LSP-AB, from node A to node B across several intermediate nodes. Node A sends a Path message for LSP-AB with the stitching desired bit. B replies in the Resv with the stitching ready bit in the RRO. Only then can A use LSP-AB for stitching.

When the Path message for LSP1-2 reaches A, A checks that the switching types match, then sends the Path message, via IP routing if needed, to B with the IF_ID RSVP_HOP identifying LSP-AB. B propagates it to R2. B returns a Label in the Resv, which A ignores before passing the Resv to R1. Each end then sets up its data plane to swap labels, giving a series of label swaps from R1 to R2.

If LSP-AB was advertised as a TE link in the same domain, R1 can compute a path over it. If R1 and A are in different domains, LSP-AB is not advertised outside the domain, and R1 would use per-domain path computation (RFC 5152) or PCE-based computation.
sections.eli5: Two helpers at the ends of a short road agree to be ready. Then a traveler arrives, goes in one end and comes out the other, and the helpers hand it on along the long road.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The changes follow those of RFC 4206: the control interface carrying RSVP messages need not be the data interface used for switching. Because those interfaces may change as routing changes, they cannot anchor security associations between neighbors, so security associations MUST be bound to the communicating neighbors themselves.

RFC 2747 offers a solution: an IP address is a valid key identifier, so the 'sending interface' can be read as 'receiver's IP address'. Since Path and PathTear messages can now be addressed to the next hop node, the IPsec Authentication Header, which RFC 2747 ruled out, becomes applicable and standard IPsec procedures can secure the exchanges.
sections.eli5: The secret handshake between neighbors is tied to who they are, not to which door the message used.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA allocated Bit Number 5 in the Attributes Flags TLV of the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object for the LSP stitching bit. It is only for use in a Path message. The matching 'LSP segment stitching ready' bit, also Bit Number 5, is used in the RRO Attributes subobject.

IANA also assigned error sub-code 30, Stitching unsupported, under the RSVP error code Routing Problem (24). It is to be used only in a PathErr.
sections.eli5: The new signals were given official numbers so everyone uses the same ones.
